# Logic for Computer Scientists

Four machines decide the same question — *does this follow from that* — and the test suite
makes them agree. Python 3.12+, standard library only, **127 tests**, clean-room from the
fifteen-lecture syllabus of the first-semester logic course (INZ001518).

## Why four

Soundness and completeness are the theorems that say a truth table, a Gentzen sequent
calculus, resolution and SLD resolution must give the same verdict. In the lecture they are
proofs about the systems; here they are an assertion that can fail, which is
[[dual-implementation-as-cross-check]] taken to four implementations that share no code.

`tests/test_proof_systems.py` runs sixteen formulas — ten valid, six not — through three of
them and asserts agreement formula by formula. The fourth appears in the demo, where the same
entailment is a two-clause logic program. A disagreement would not be an interesting result;
it would be a bug in one of the four.

## A failed proof is more useful than a `False`

When the sequent calculus cannot close a branch, only atoms remain on it: those on the left
must be true and those on the right false. That open branch **is** a countermodel, and the
suite reads the valuation off the failed proof and checks that it falsifies the formula. A
prover that returns a bare "not provable" throws that away.

## Equivalent, equisatisfiable, and the price of each

Two constructions weaken equivalence to equisatisfiability for the same reason — see
[[equisatisfiable-not-equivalent]]:

- **Tseitin.** CNF by distribution is *equivalent* and exponential: `(a₁ & b₁) | … | (aₙ & bₙ)`
  has exactly `2ⁿ` clauses, which the suite asserts as a count rather than a tendency. Naming
  each subformula with a fresh variable gives a CNF that is linear and merely equisatisfiable
  — under sixty clauses against 256 at `n = 8`.
- **Skolemisation.** Replacing `∃y` by a function of the universally quantified variables in
  scope removes the existentials and changes the signature, so it cannot be equivalent. It is
  enough for refutation, which is why every first-order prover starts there.

## Boundaries in signatures, not in caveats

Every method here has a point past which it stops working, and each is expressed in the API:

| Module | Boundary | How it shows up |
|---|---|---|
| `truth` | `2ⁿ` valuations | `MAX_ENUMERABLE_VARIABLES = 20`; past it a `ValueError` naming the row count |
| `resolution` | exponential saturation | `max_steps`; exceeding it raises, never returns "not refutable" |
| `prolog` | SLD is incomplete under a fixed clause order | `DepthExceeded`, distinct from "no solutions" |
| `predicate` | first-order validity is undecidable | there is no `is_valid`; `is_valid_in` takes an explicit family of structures |

"Out of budget" and "no answer" are different facts, and conflating them is how a prover lies.

## The bug that changed the design

The grammar module's first membership algorithm searched forward from the start symbol and
pruned any sentential form longer than the target. **It hung.** With `S → S S | ε` the form
`S S S S` is longer than the target and can still shrink back to it, so nothing was ever
prunable. A step cap would have converted the hang into a spurious "not in the language".

The fix was to transform the input instead: remove epsilon and unit productions first, after
which every derivation step either lengthens the form or consumes a nonterminal, and the
bounded search becomes a genuine decision procedure. Recorded as
[[transform-the-input-rather-than-cap-the-search]].

## The fifteen lectures, as modules

Sets, relations, orders and functions (1–3) in `relations.py`; formal languages and
context-free grammars (4) in `grammar.py`; many-sorted algebras and relational systems (5) in
`algebra.py`; propositional syntax and semantics (6–7) across `formula.py`, `parse.py` and
`truth.py`; the Gentzen system (8) in `gentzen.py`; functional completeness and metalogic (9)
in `connectives.py`; the predicate calculus (10–12) and canonical forms (13) in
`predicate.py` and `normal.py`; resolution (14) in `resolution.py`; logic programming (15) in
`prolog.py`.

Functional completeness is decided twice: **Post's criterion** reports *which* of the five
closed classes swallows an incomplete set — `{&, |}` fails because both are monotone and no
composition of monotone functions is anything else — and `to_nand` decides it constructively
by rewriting any formula into nands.

## 2026-08-12 reference audit

Python compilation, **127/127** standard-library tests, and the headless demo passed. The
demo confirmed agreement among the truth table, Gentzen, resolution, and SLD resolution for
the documented entailment; it also produced the tested normal-form, countermodel, grammar,
and relation examples. The existing four-machine visual guide is retained because it follows
that reproducible demonstration and states the methods' boundaries.

## Status and provenance

Local repository on `main`, one commit, **not pushed**. The course reading included a
third-party logic textbook; it was not consulted and nothing from it appears here, which
`NOTICE` states explicitly — see [[provenance-notice-file]] and
[[clean-room-rebuild-from-specification]]. `TASKS.md` lists the intended next steps: DPLL

calculus.
